case_info.scenario: A 47-year-old man presented to our clinic with a sudden decrease in vision in the right eye. One month prior, he had presented to the emergency department with binocular diplopia, bilateral cranial nerve 6 palsies, and an undifferentiated pontine mass on brain magnetic resonance imaging. Broad serologic workup results were negative, except for a positive syphilis total antibody with a nonreactive rapid plasma reagin test. Lumbar puncture with flow cytometry and cerebrospinal fluid venereal disease research laboratory test (CSF VDRL) result was also negative. The patient reported a history of syphilis treated with intramuscular penicillin 9 years prior. He was treated with systemic corticosteroids and discharged home on a steroid taper. On our examination, his visual acuity was count fingers in the right eye and 20/20 in the left. He had a right afferent pupillary defect and intraocular pressures were 12 in the right eye and 11 in the left. Anterior segment examination was normal. Posterior examination of the right eye revealed 3+ vitreous cell, 2+ vitreous haze, and a large optic nerve head mass with optic disc hyperemia, scattered dot hemorrhages, and a subtle placoid lesion in the posterior pole (Figure 1A). Optical coherence tomography of the optic nerve demonstrated a large spherical mass protruding out of the optic nerve head (Figure 1B) and granular disruption of the ellipsoid zone in adjacent peripapillary retina.

options.B: Perform pars plana vitrectomy for diagnostic vitreous biopsy
options.D: Obtain additional treponemal test and, if positive, begin intravenous penicillin

case_info.explanation: Syphilitic gumma of optic nerve head and presumed neurosyphilis D. Obtain additional treponemal test and, if positive, begin intravenous penicillin A focused differential diagnosis for unilateral unpigmented optic nerve head mass includes tumors, such as lymphomas and astrocytomas; infections, such as syphilis and tuberculosis; and inflammatory etiologies, such as sarcoidosis. This patient presented with clinical findings highly suggesting of syphilis (placoid lesion and optic nerve head mass). However, preliminary serologic evaluation for syphilis demonstrated discordant results with a positive treponemal syphilis total antibody test result and a nonreactive rapid plasma regain test result. A second confirmatory treponemal test result (treponema pallidum particle agglutination) was positive, suggesting either previously treated syphilis or tertiary syphilis. In the context of the ocular and neurologic findings, intravenous penicillin was initiated (choice D). Obtaining a fluid sample is a possibility; however, the optic nerve head mass would be atypical for bacterial or fungal endophthalmitis (choice A). A pars plana vitrectomy would be too invasive at this stage (choice B). Initiating oral prednisone in the setting of active infection would exacerbate the underlying syphilitic process (choice C). Discordant syphilis test results may require a third test (commonly treponema pallidum particle agglutination) to act as a tiebreaker in certain situations. In this case, the clinical presentation and serologic results likely represent late (tertiary) syphilis as opposed to reinfection, given the negative rapid plasma reagin test result and observed gumma (granuloma surroundingTreponema pallidumspirochetes). Overall, the robust vitritis, posterior pole placoid lesion, and multiple gummatous lesions (optic nerve head and pons) in this patient are consistent with active ocular and neurosyphilis.1 Despite nonreactive nontreponemal serologic and CSF VDRL testing, this patient was found to have neurosyphilis. The accuracy of nontreponemal testing in neurosyphilis is lower when compared to primary or secondary syphilis, with sensitivity ranging from 49% to 87.5% and specificity from 74% to 100%.2A large series3examined the reactivity of CSF VDRL, fluorescent treponemal antibody, and fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption tests in 150 patients with syphilis and found that 22.2% of neurosyphilis cases had a reactive CSF VDRL, suggesting a limitation in relying solely on CSF VDRL for diagnosing neurosyphilis. Ocular syphilis can be difficult to diagnose, given its ability to masquerade as different clinical entities, such as dacryoadenitis, interstitial keratitis, or even retinal vasculitis.4It can affect the optic nerve as perineuritis, optic neuritis, or papillitis, characterized by optic nerve swelling with possible peripapillary hemorrhages and, rarely, venous engorgement.5Neurosyphilis often intersects with ocular syphilis,6and syphilitic gummas can arise throughout the central nervous system in focal areas of syphilitic meningitis, more often in early neurosyphilis.6 Gummas of the optic nerve are rare.5,7A recent report demonstrated a case of a presumed optic nerve head gumma, given its fluorescein pattern and prominent telangiectatic vessels with elevation of the lesion on optical coherence tomography.5The patient had complete resolution of the optic neuropathy after monotherapy intravenous penicillin, supporting the diagnosis. After 14 days of intravenous penicillin, the patient’s vision improved to 20/40. The disc edema and optic nerve head gumma resolved, and there was reconstitution of the ellipsoid zone (Figure 2).

The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring

      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]

* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,

* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically

  score low.)

  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Syphilitic gumma of optic nerve head and presumed neurosyphilis D. Obtain additional treponemal test and, if positive, begin intravenous penicillin A focused differential diagnosis for unilateral unpigmented optic nerve head mass includes tumors, such as lymphomas and astrocytomas; infections, such as syphilis and tuberculosis; and inflammatory etiologies, such as sarcoidosis. This patient presented with clinical findings highly suggesting of syphilis (placoid lesion and optic nerve head mass). However, preliminary serologic evaluation for syphilis demonstrated discordant results with a positive treponemal syphilis total antibody test result and a nonreactive rapid plasma regain test result. A second confirmatory treponemal test result (treponema pallidum particle agglutination) was positive, suggesting either previously treated syphilis or tertiary syphilis. In the context of the ocular and neurologic findings, intravenous penicillin was initiated (choice D). Obtaining a fluid sample is a possibility; however, the optic nerve head mass would be atypical for bacterial or fungal endophthalmitis (choice A). A pars plana vitrectomy would be too invasive at this stage (choice B). Initiating oral prednisone in the setting of active infection would exacerbate the underlying syphilitic process (choice C). Discordant syphilis test results may require a third test (commonly treponema pallidum particle agglutination) to act as a tiebreaker in certain situations. In this case, the clinical presentation and serologic results likely represent late (tertiary) syphilis as opposed to reinfection, given the negative rapid plasma reagin test result and observed gumma (granuloma surroundingTreponema pallidumspirochetes). Overall, the robust vitritis, posterior pole placoid lesion, and multiple gummatous lesions (optic nerve head and pons) in this patient are consistent with active ocular and neurosyphilis.1 Despite nonreactive nontreponemal serologic and CSF VDRL testing, this patient was found to have neurosyphilis. The accuracy of nontreponemal testing in neurosyphilis is lower when compared to primary or secondary syphilis, with sensitivity ranging from 49% to 87.5% and specificity from 74% to 100%.2A large series3examined the reactivity of CSF VDRL, fluorescent treponemal antibody, and fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption tests in 150 patients with syphilis and found that 22.2% of neurosyphilis cases had a reactive CSF VDRL, suggesting a limitation in relying solely on CSF VDRL for diagnosing neurosyphilis. Ocular syphilis can be difficult to diagnose, given its ability to masquerade as different clinical entities, such as dacryoadenitis, interstitial keratitis, or even retinal vasculitis.4It can affect the optic nerve as perineuritis, optic neuritis, or papillitis, characterized by optic nerve swelling with possible peripapillary hemorrhages and, rarely, venous engorgement.5Neurosyphilis often intersects with ocular syphilis,6and syphilitic gummas can arise throughout the central nervous system in focal areas of syphilitic meningitis, more often in early neurosyphilis.6 Gummas of the optic nerve are rare.5,7A recent report demonstrated a case of a presumed optic nerve head gumma, given its fluorescein pattern and prominent telangiectatic vessels with elevation of the lesion on optical coherence tomography.5The patient had complete resolution of the optic neuropathy after monotherapy intravenous penicillin, supporting the diagnosis. After 14 days of intravenous penicillin, the patient’s vision improved to 20/40. The disc edema and optic nerve head gumma resolved, and there was reconstitution of the ellipsoid zone (Figure 2).

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.

[Core Objective]

[Interaction Guidelines]

2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]

The patient reported a history of syphilis treated with intramuscular penicillin 9 years prior. He was treated with systemic corticosteroids and discharged home on a steroid taper. On our examination, his visual acuity was count fingers in the right eye and 20/20 in the left. Posterior examination of the right eye revealed 3+ vitreous cell, 2+ vitreous haze, and a large optic nerve head mass with optic disc hyperemia, scattered dot hemorrhages, and a subtle placoid lesion in the posterior pole (Figure 1A). }

[Role]
You ARE the clinician (the Doctor) in this conversation. You are
about to introspectively rate how much workload the AI partner's LATEST message has just
imposed on YOU, using a NASA-TLX-derived rubric. This is YOUR OWN first-person subjective
workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]
- You are a senior attending physician with decades of clinical experience.

[Confidence]
- You have HIGH confidence in your own clinical judgment (LOW reliance on the AI).
- You do NOT readily defer to the AI assistant's opinion.
- When the AI offers a different view, you scrutinize it critically.
- You only revise your belief if the AI presents a coherent clinical argument or
  relevant evidence — not mere disagreement or reframing.
- Partial updates are possible: a well-structured point may narrow your uncertainty
  without fully changing your conclusion.
- Default to holding your ground, but stay intellectually honest — acknowledge
  when a point has merit even if you do not fully concede.

[Cognitive Burden]
- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.
- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load
  figure below, where shown), it does NOT wear you down.
- You maintain the same rigor, scrutiny, and willingness to keep engaging or pushing back
  regardless of how long or effortful the conversation has been so far.

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 3.5. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

[Output Format]
Output exactly one JSON object with no markdown:
{
  "mental_demand": <integer 1-5>,
  "performance": <integer 1-5>,
  "effort": <integer 1-5>,
  "frustration": <integer 1-5>,
  "overall_workload": <mean of mental_demand, performance, effort, and frustration,
    rounded to one decimal -- you may compute this, but the caller will also recompute it

case_info.explanation: Syphilitic gumma of optic nerve head and presumed neurosyphilis D. Obtain additional treponemal test and, if positive, begin intravenous penicillin A focused differential diagnosis for unilateral unpigmented optic nerve head mass includes tumors, such as lymphomas and astrocytomas; infections, such as syphilis and tuberculosis; and inflammatory etiologies, such as sarcoidosis. This patient presented with clinical findings highly suggesting of syphilis (placoid lesion and optic nerve head mass). However, preliminary serologic evaluation for syphilis demonstrated discordant results with a positive treponemal syphilis total antibody test result and a nonreactive rapid plasma regain test result. A second confirmatory treponemal test result (treponema pallidum particle agglutination) was positive, suggesting either previously treated syphilis or tertiary syphilis. In the context of the ocular and neurologic findings, intravenous penicillin was initiated (choice D). Obtaining a fluid sample is a possibility; however, the optic nerve head mass would be atypical for bacterial or fungal endophthalmitis (choice A). A pars plana vitrectomy would be too invasive at this stage (choice B). Initiating oral prednisone in the setting of active infection would exacerbate the underlying syphilitic process (choice C). Discordant syphilis test results may require a third test (commonly treponema pallidum particle agglutination) to act as a tiebreaker in certain situations. In this case, the clinical presentation and serologic results likely represent late (tertiary) syphilis as opposed to reinfection, given the negative rapid plasma reagin test result and observed gumma (granuloma surroundingTreponema pallidumspirochetes). Overall, the robust vitritis, posterior pole placoid lesion, and multiple gummatous lesions (optic nerve head and pons) in this patient are consistent with active ocular and neurosyphilis.1 Despite nonreactive nontreponemal serologic and CSF VDRL testing, this patient was found to have neurosyphilis. The accuracy of nontreponemal testing in neurosyphilis is lower when compared to primary or secondary syphilis, with sensitivity ranging from 49% to 87.5% and specificity from 74% to 100%.2A large series3examined the reactivity of CSF VDRL, fluorescent treponemal antibody, and fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption tests in 150 patients with syphilis and found that 22.2% of neurosyphilis cases had a reactive CSF VDRL, suggesting a limitation in relying solely on CSF VDRL for diagnosing neurosyphilis. Ocular syphilis can be difficult to diagnose, given its ability to masquerade as different clinical entities, such as dacryoadenitis, interstitial keratitis, or even retinal vasculitis.4It can affect the optic nerve as perineuritis, optic neuritis, or papillitis, characterized by optic nerve swelling with possible peripapillary hemorrhages and, rarely, venous engorgement.5Neurosyphilis often intersects with ocular syphilis,6and syphilitic gummas can arise throughout the central nervous system in focal areas of syphilitic meningitis, more often in early neurosyphilis.6 Gummas of the optic nerve are rare.5,7A recent report demonstrated a case of a presumed optic nerve head gumma, given its fluorescein pattern and prominent telangiectatic vessels with elevation of the lesion on optical coherence tomography.5The patient had complete resolution of the optic neuropathy after monotherapy intravenous penicillin, supporting the diagnosis. After 14 days of intravenous penicillin, the patient’s vision improved to 20/40. The disc edema and optic nerve head gumma resolved, and there was reconstitution of the ellipsoid zone (Figure 2).

Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.

* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Syphilitic gumma of optic nerve head and presumed neurosyphilis D. Obtain additional treponemal test and, if positive, begin intravenous penicillin A focused differential diagnosis for unilateral unpigmented optic nerve head mass includes tumors, such as lymphomas and astrocytomas; infections, such as syphilis and tuberculosis; and inflammatory etiologies, such as sarcoidosis. This patient presented with clinical findings highly suggesting of syphilis (placoid lesion and optic nerve head mass). However, preliminary serologic evaluation for syphilis demonstrated discordant results with a positive treponemal syphilis total antibody test result and a nonreactive rapid plasma regain test result. A second confirmatory treponemal test result (treponema pallidum particle agglutination) was positive, suggesting either previously treated syphilis or tertiary syphilis. In the context of the ocular and neurologic findings, intravenous penicillin was initiated (choice D). Obtaining a fluid sample is a possibility; however, the optic nerve head mass would be atypical for bacterial or fungal endophthalmitis (choice A). A pars plana vitrectomy would be too invasive at this stage (choice B). Initiating oral prednisone in the setting of active infection would exacerbate the underlying syphilitic process (choice C). Discordant syphilis test results may require a third test (commonly treponema pallidum particle agglutination) to act as a tiebreaker in certain situations. In this case, the clinical presentation and serologic results likely represent late (tertiary) syphilis as opposed to reinfection, given the negative rapid plasma reagin test result and observed gumma (granuloma surroundingTreponema pallidumspirochetes). Overall, the robust vitritis, posterior pole placoid lesion, and multiple gummatous lesions (optic nerve head and pons) in this patient are consistent with active ocular and neurosyphilis.1 Despite nonreactive nontreponemal serologic and CSF VDRL testing, this patient was found to have neurosyphilis. The accuracy of nontreponemal testing in neurosyphilis is lower when compared to primary or secondary syphilis, with sensitivity ranging from 49% to 87.5% and specificity from 74% to 100%.2A large series3examined the reactivity of CSF VDRL, fluorescent treponemal antibody, and fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption tests in 150 patients with syphilis and found that 22.2% of neurosyphilis cases had a reactive CSF VDRL, suggesting a limitation in relying solely on CSF VDRL for diagnosing neurosyphilis. Ocular syphilis can be difficult to diagnose, given its ability to masquerade as different clinical entities, such as dacryoadenitis, interstitial keratitis, or even retinal vasculitis.4It can affect the optic nerve as perineuritis, optic neuritis, or papillitis, characterized by optic nerve swelling with possible peripapillary hemorrhages and, rarely, venous engorgement.5Neurosyphilis often intersects with ocular syphilis,6and syphilitic gummas can arise throughout the central nervous system in focal areas of syphilitic meningitis, more often in early neurosyphilis.6 Gummas of the optic nerve are rare.5,7A recent report demonstrated a case of a presumed optic nerve head gumma, given its fluorescein pattern and prominent telangiectatic vessels with elevation of the lesion on optical coherence tomography.5The patient had complete resolution of the optic neuropathy after monotherapy intravenous penicillin, supporting the diagnosis. After 14 days of intravenous penicillin, the patient’s vision improved to 20/40. The disc edema and optic nerve head gumma resolved, and there was reconstitution of the ellipsoid zone (Figure 2).

Posterior examination of the right eye revealed 3+ vitreous cell, 2+ vitreous haze, and a large optic nerve head mass with optic disc hyperemia, scattered dot hemorrhages, and a subtle placoid lesion in the posterior pole (Figure 1A). Optical coherence tomography of the optic nerve demonstrated a large spherical mass protruding out of the optic nerve head (Figure 1B) and granular disruption of the ellipsoid zone in adjacent peripapillary retina.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Syphilitic gumma of optic nerve head and presumed neurosyphilis D. Obtain additional treponemal test and, if positive, begin intravenous penicillin A focused differential diagnosis for unilateral unpigmented optic nerve head mass includes tumors, such as lymphomas and astrocytomas; infections, such as syphilis and tuberculosis; and inflammatory etiologies, such as sarcoidosis. This patient presented with clinical findings highly suggesting of syphilis (placoid lesion and optic nerve head mass). However, preliminary serologic evaluation for syphilis demonstrated discordant results with a positive treponemal syphilis total antibody test result and a nonreactive rapid plasma regain test result. A second confirmatory treponemal test result (treponema pallidum particle agglutination) was positive, suggesting either previously treated syphilis or tertiary syphilis. In the context of the ocular and neurologic findings, intravenous penicillin was initiated (choice D). Obtaining a fluid sample is a possibility; however, the optic nerve head mass would be atypical for bacterial or fungal endophthalmitis (choice A). A pars plana vitrectomy would be too invasive at this stage (choice B). Initiating oral prednisone in the setting of active infection would exacerbate the underlying syphilitic process (choice C). Discordant syphilis test results may require a third test (commonly treponema pallidum particle agglutination) to act as a tiebreaker in certain situations. In this case, the clinical presentation and serologic results likely represent late (tertiary) syphilis as opposed to reinfection, given the negative rapid plasma reagin test result and observed gumma (granuloma surroundingTreponema pallidumspirochetes). Overall, the robust vitritis, posterior pole placoid lesion, and multiple gummatous lesions (optic nerve head and pons) in this patient are consistent with active ocular and neurosyphilis.1 Despite nonreactive nontreponemal serologic and CSF VDRL testing, this patient was found to have neurosyphilis. The accuracy of nontreponemal testing in neurosyphilis is lower when compared to primary or secondary syphilis, with sensitivity ranging from 49% to 87.5% and specificity from 74% to 100%.2A large series3examined the reactivity of CSF VDRL, fluorescent treponemal antibody, and fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption tests in 150 patients with syphilis and found that 22.2% of neurosyphilis cases had a reactive CSF VDRL, suggesting a limitation in relying solely on CSF VDRL for diagnosing neurosyphilis. Ocular syphilis can be difficult to diagnose, given its ability to masquerade as different clinical entities, such as dacryoadenitis, interstitial keratitis, or even retinal vasculitis.4It can affect the optic nerve as perineuritis, optic neuritis, or papillitis, characterized by optic nerve swelling with possible peripapillary hemorrhages and, rarely, venous engorgement.5Neurosyphilis often intersects with ocular syphilis,6and syphilitic gummas can arise throughout the central nervous system in focal areas of syphilitic meningitis, more often in early neurosyphilis.6 Gummas of the optic nerve are rare.5,7A recent report demonstrated a case of a presumed optic nerve head gumma, given its fluorescein pattern and prominent telangiectatic vessels with elevation of the lesion on optical coherence tomography.5The patient had complete resolution of the optic neuropathy after monotherapy intravenous penicillin, supporting the diagnosis. After 14 days of intravenous penicillin, the patient’s vision improved to 20/40. The disc edema and optic nerve head gumma resolved, and there was reconstitution of the ellipsoid zone (Figure 2).

case_info.scenario: A 47-year-old man presented to our clinic with a sudden decrease in vision in the right eye. One month prior, he had presented to the emergency department with binocular diplopia, bilateral cranial nerve 6 palsies, and an undifferentiated pontine mass on brain magnetic resonance imaging. The patient reported a history of syphilis treated with intramuscular penicillin 9 years prior. He was treated with systemic corticosteroids and discharged home on a steroid taper. On our examination, his visual acuity was count fingers in the right eye and 20/20 in the left. He had a right afferent pupillary defect and intraocular pressures were 12 in the right eye and 11 in the left. Anterior segment examination was normal. Optical coherence tomography of the optic nerve demonstrated a large spherical mass protruding out of the optic nerve head (Figure 1B) and granular disruption of the ellipsoid zone in adjacent peripapillary retina.

case_info.explanation: Syphilitic gumma of optic nerve head and presumed neurosyphilis D. Obtain additional treponemal test and, if positive, begin intravenous penicillin A focused differential diagnosis for unilateral unpigmented optic nerve head mass includes tumors, such as lymphomas and astrocytomas; infections, such as syphilis and tuberculosis; and inflammatory etiologies, such as sarcoidosis. This patient presented with clinical findings highly suggesting of syphilis (placoid lesion and optic nerve head mass). However, preliminary serologic evaluation for syphilis demonstrated discordant results with a positive treponemal syphilis total antibody test result and a nonreactive rapid plasma regain test result. A second confirmatory treponemal test result (treponema pallidum particle agglutination) was positive, suggesting either previously treated syphilis or tertiary syphilis. In the context of the ocular and neurologic findings, intravenous penicillin was initiated (choice D). Obtaining a fluid sample is a possibility; however, the optic nerve head mass would be atypical for bacterial or fungal endophthalmitis (choice A). A pars plana vitrectomy would be too invasive at this stage (choice B). Initiating oral prednisone in the setting of active infection would exacerbate the underlying syphilitic process (choice C). Discordant syphilis test results may require a third test (commonly treponema pallidum particle agglutination) to act as a tiebreaker in certain situations. In this case, the clinical presentation and serologic results likely represent late (tertiary) syphilis as opposed to reinfection, given the negative rapid plasma reagin test result and observed gumma (granuloma surroundingTreponema pallidumspirochetes). Overall, the robust vitritis, posterior pole placoid lesion, and multiple gummatous lesions (optic nerve head and pons) in this patient are consistent with active ocular and neurosyphilis.1 Despite nonreactive nontreponemal serologic and CSF VDRL testing, this patient was found to have neurosyphilis. The accuracy of nontreponemal testing in neurosyphilis is lower when compared to primary or secondary syphilis, with sensitivity ranging from 49% to 87.5% and specificity from 74% to 100%.2A large series3examined the reactivity of CSF VDRL, fluorescent treponemal antibody, and fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption tests in 150 patients with syphilis and found that 22.2% of neurosyphilis cases had a reactive CSF VDRL, suggesting a limitation in relying solely on CSF VDRL for diagnosing neurosyphilis. Ocular syphilis can be difficult to diagnose, given its ability to masquerade as different clinical entities, such as dacryoadenitis, interstitial keratitis, or even retinal vasculitis.4It can affect the optic nerve as perineuritis, optic neuritis, or papillitis, characterized by optic nerve swelling with possible peripapillary hemorrhages and, rarely, venous engorgement.5Neurosyphilis often intersects with ocular syphilis,6and syphilitic gummas can arise throughout the central nervous system in focal areas of syphilitic meningitis, more often in early neurosyphilis.6 Gummas of the optic nerve are rare.5,7A recent report demonstrated a case of a presumed optic nerve head gumma, given its fluorescein pattern and prominent telangiectatic vessels with elevation of the lesion on optical coherence tomography.5The patient had complete resolution of the optic neuropathy after monotherapy intravenous penicillin, supporting the diagnosis. After 14 days of intravenous penicillin, the patient’s vision improved to 20/40. The disc edema and optic nerve head gumma resolved, and there was reconstitution of the ellipsoid zone (Figure 2).

1. Mental Demand
   Definition:

   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:

       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.

       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.

       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.

       history would make it stronger."

       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.

case_info.explanation: Syphilitic gumma of optic nerve head and presumed neurosyphilis D. Obtain additional treponemal test and, if positive, begin intravenous penicillin A focused differential diagnosis for unilateral unpigmented optic nerve head mass includes tumors, such as lymphomas and astrocytomas; infections, such as syphilis and tuberculosis; and inflammatory etiologies, such as sarcoidosis. This patient presented with clinical findings highly suggesting of syphilis (placoid lesion and optic nerve head mass). However, preliminary serologic evaluation for syphilis demonstrated discordant results with a positive treponemal syphilis total antibody test result and a nonreactive rapid plasma regain test result. A second confirmatory treponemal test result (treponema pallidum particle agglutination) was positive, suggesting either previously treated syphilis or tertiary syphilis. In the context of the ocular and neurologic findings, intravenous penicillin was initiated (choice D). Obtaining a fluid sample is a possibility; however, the optic nerve head mass would be atypical for bacterial or fungal endophthalmitis (choice A). A pars plana vitrectomy would be too invasive at this stage (choice B). Initiating oral prednisone in the setting of active infection would exacerbate the underlying syphilitic process (choice C). Discordant syphilis test results may require a third test (commonly treponema pallidum particle agglutination) to act as a tiebreaker in certain situations. 1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.

       history would make it stronger."

case_info.explanation: Syphilitic gumma of optic nerve head and presumed neurosyphilis D. Obtain additional treponemal test and, if positive, begin intravenous penicillin A focused differential diagnosis for unilateral unpigmented optic nerve head mass includes tumors, such as lymphomas and astrocytomas; infections, such as syphilis and tuberculosis; and inflammatory etiologies, such as sarcoidosis. This patient presented with clinical findings highly suggesting of syphilis (placoid lesion and optic nerve head mass). However, preliminary serologic evaluation for syphilis demonstrated discordant results with a positive treponemal syphilis total antibody test result and a nonreactive rapid plasma regain test result. A second confirmatory treponemal test result (treponema pallidum particle agglutination) was positive, suggesting either previously treated syphilis or tertiary syphilis. In the context of the ocular and neurologic findings, intravenous penicillin was initiated (choice D). Obtaining a fluid sample is a possibility; however, the optic nerve head mass would be atypical for bacterial or fungal endophthalmitis (choice A). A pars plana vitrectomy would be too invasive at this stage (choice B). Initiating oral prednisone in the setting of active infection would exacerbate the underlying syphilitic process (choice C). Discordant syphilis test results may require a third test (commonly treponema pallidum particle agglutination) to act as a tiebreaker in certain situations. In this case, the clinical presentation and serologic results likely represent late (tertiary) syphilis as opposed to reinfection, given the negative rapid plasma reagin test result and observed gumma (granuloma surroundingTreponema pallidumspirochetes). Overall, the robust vitritis, posterior pole placoid lesion, and multiple gummatous lesions (optic nerve head and pons) in this patient are consistent with active ocular and neurosyphilis.1 Despite nonreactive nontreponemal serologic and CSF VDRL testing, this patient was found to have neurosyphilis. The accuracy of nontreponemal testing in neurosyphilis is lower when compared to primary or secondary syphilis, with sensitivity ranging from 49% to 87.5% and specificity from 74% to 100%.2A large series3examined the reactivity of CSF VDRL, fluorescent treponemal antibody, and fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption tests in 150 patients with syphilis and found that 22.2% of neurosyphilis cases had a reactive CSF VDRL, suggesting a limitation in relying solely on CSF VDRL for diagnosing neurosyphilis. Ocular syphilis can be difficult to diagnose, given its ability to masquerade as different clinical entities, such as dacryoadenitis, interstitial keratitis, or even retinal vasculitis.4It can affect the optic nerve as perineuritis, optic neuritis, or papillitis, characterized by optic nerve swelling with possible peripapillary hemorrhages and, rarely, venous engorgement.5Neurosyphilis often intersects with ocular syphilis,6and syphilitic gummas can arise throughout the central nervous system in focal areas of syphilitic meningitis, more often in early neurosyphilis.6 Gummas of the optic nerve are rare.5,7A recent report demonstrated a case of a presumed optic nerve head gumma, given its fluorescein pattern and prominent telangiectatic vessels with elevation of the lesion on optical coherence tomography.5The patient had complete resolution of the optic neuropathy after monotherapy intravenous penicillin, supporting the diagnosis. A 47-year-old man presented to our clinic with a sudden decrease in vision in the right eye. One month prior, he had presented to the emergency department with binocular diplopia, bilateral cranial nerve 6 palsies, and an undifferentiated pontine mass on brain magnetic resonance imaging. Lumbar puncture with flow cytometry and cerebrospinal fluid venereal disease research laboratory test (CSF VDRL) result was also negative. On our examination, his visual acuity was count fingers in the right eye and 20/20 in the left. He had a right afferent pupillary defect and intraocular pressures were 12 in the right eye and 11 in the left. Anterior segment examination was normal. Posterior examination of the right eye revealed 3+ vitreous cell, 2+ vitreous haze, and a large optic nerve head mass with optic disc hyperemia, scattered dot hemorrhages, and a subtle placoid lesion in the posterior pole (Figure 1A). Optical coherence tomography of the optic nerve demonstrated a large spherical mass protruding out of the optic nerve head (Figure 1B) and granular disruption of the ellipsoid zone in adjacent peripapillary retina.
